notes:
I found less than I hoped for parts 2 and 3. I did not reach netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or catholic.com. None of the pages I read were written by prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teachers. The Catholic notes below come from Haydock's commentary (hosted on studylight.org) and the Catholic Encyclopedia on newadvent.org. On this chapter, the Protestant teachers I read mostly differ in shades of emphasis, not in real disagreements. I've marked those spots below.

**v. 1–2**
- Wesley (Methodist) says Job accepts God's unlimited power, knowledge and rule, which was the point of God's speech from the whirlwind. Once his mind was convinced, his conscience was too: he saw how foolish his irreverent words had been. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Guzik ties "You can do everything" to God's power over creation, and also to the comfort Job felt in God's presence while still not understanding his crisis. The God who masters Behemoth and Leviathan can carry out every purpose in Job's life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/

**v. 3**
- Guzik says Job had said many sad and unwise things, in his cry of chapter 3 and in the debate. He now comes back to humble contentment with not knowing the answers. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: Job's words about God were mostly true, but he had spoken beyond what he could know. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Wesley paraphrases it as "I have spoken foolishly and unadvisedly of all things far above my reach." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Catholic (Haydock): He does not accuse himself of any sin or false assertion, but acknowledges his infirmity in not having understood this before. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job-42.html

**v. 4**
- Wesley says Job hands God's challenging words back to Him as words of surrender. Job will stop arguing and ask to be taught instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Guzik: Before, Job seemed to want to challenge God (Job 31:35-40) in a confrontational way. Now, after his wonderful revelation of God, He respectfully asked God for the right to speak. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/

**v. 5**
- Guzik says what changed Job most was God's loving presence, more than anything God said. Job "saw" God, though not with his literal eyes. His earlier knowledge wasn't false, but it now looked pale beside this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Wesley says Job's knowledge of God had rested mainly on what people taught him. Now God's appearing and the Holy Spirit had made it clear and certain, as if seen with bodily eyes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Job saw not God's face ( Exd 33:20 ), but His presence in the veil of a dark cloud. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_042.cfm
- Keil and Delitzsch, quoted on Bible Hub, say this is the first time Job truly perceives God, through direct contact with Him rather than tradition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-6.htm

**v. 6** (the main place where readers differ: "despise myself" or "retract my words"?)
- Older readings stress real sorrow for sin:
  - Barnes says Job had thought too highly of his own righteousness and defended his integrity in language he couldn't justify. He now takes the lowest place. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/42-6.html
  - Barnes adds a limit: Job had no need to repent of his main views, which God later says were correct (v. 8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-6.htm
  - Matthew Henry says Job's afflictions first brought him to the ashes, but now his sins brought him there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/42-6.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) lists what Job repented of: cursing the day he was born, wishing to die, his complaints and his suspicions of God. Spurgeon also notes the Hebrew word has just a tinge of comfort, and that Job's repentance was the sign of his deliverance. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/job-among-the-ashes
- The "retraction" reading:
  - Guzik cites Smick, Morgan and Andersen. The word "myself" isn't in the Hebrew, and the verb can mean "I reject what I said." This is regret for hasty words, not the self-loathing that goes with confessing known sins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
  - The Cambridge Bible likewise says the word means I retract, or repudiate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-6.htm
- Guzik stresses that Job did *not* admit his friends were right. He repented of sins committed after the disaster began, not sins that caused it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Ligonier (Reformed) says Job erred in believing the Lord owed him a full explanation of his suffering. Sitting in ashes showed that God was right. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jobs-repentance-and-restoration
- Constable says Job had previously expressed remorse over his losses, but now he grieved over his sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/42-6.html
- GotQuestions says dust stands for nothingness and humility. Mourning in dust and ashes was an ancient custom, not a biblical command. https://www.gotquestions.org/repent-dust-ashes.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik says the friends' general principles were wise in themselves but didn't fit Job's case. They presented God as angry with Job when He was not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Elihu is not rebuked, and two of my sources explain this differently:
  - Wesley says Elihu was spared because he treated Job more mercifully and corrected only his words, without condemning him as a person. Wesley also reads "you have not spoken right" as a comparison: Job was less to blame because his view of providence was truer than theirs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
  - Guzik thinks God's silence toward Elihu is better read as dismissing him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Catholic (Haydock): God questioned Job because others might draw wrong conclusions from his words, But Job entertained no such ideas. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job-42.html

**v. 8**
- Wesley says God makes Job the friends' priest, to pray and offer sacrifice for them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Matthew Henry says that here Job became a type of Christ, through whom alone we and our spiritual sacrifices are acceptable to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_042.cfm
- Guzik points out the irony: Eliphaz, who urged Job to get right with God, ends up needing Job's prayers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/

**v. 9**
- Wesley: as Job prayed and offered sacrifice for those that had grieved and wounded his spirit, so Christ prayed and died for his persecutors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Guzik says the friends were accepted for Job's sake. He quotes Chambers praising them for obeying without trying to justify themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/

**v. 10** (did Job's prayer bring about his restoration?)
- Ellicott says Job's own deliverance came through the self-forgetting act of praying for others. Some sorrows are never mended in this life, and for those the hope is the Gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-10.htm
- Barnes is more cautious: It is not implied of necessity that his praying for them had any particular effect in restoring his prosperity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-10.htm
- Gill says the turn came while Job was praying, or soon after. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary both connect it to Job forgiving his friends. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-10.htm
- Guzik notes that Job never asked for his wealth back. The literal phrase "turned the captivity" means Job was in a kind of captivity until he prayed for his friends. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- On "double": Gill says it may simply mean abundance. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown see a picture of the final vindication at the resurrection. Keil and Delitzsch note that the phrase led some to read Job as a picture of Israel in exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-10.htm
- Popular "reward" reading (closest I found to prosperity teaching): Bible Hub's study note says the verse shows that God rewards faithfulness far beyond what was forfeited. https://biblehub.com/job/42-10.htm
  - A counterweight on Bible Hub's sermon page: The Christian Job may never recover his property or his health; and yet in his afflictions he may receive his greatest heritage of blessing. https://biblehub.com/sermons/job/42-10.htm
- Catholic: the Douay-Rheims reads "the Lord also was turned at the penance of Job." https://biblehub.com/job/42-10.htm Haydock quotes the Septuagint, which says God forgave the friends' sin while Job prayed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job-42.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik says these relatives had once shunned Job (19:13–14). He quotes Andersen: even with everything set right, Job still feels the hurt and needs human comfort. Poole sees the gifts as partly making up his losses and partly honouring him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Wesley says the family feasted to celebrate God's favour. They now said how they had felt about his troubles, having had no chance to say it before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm

**v. 12**
- Wesley notes the numbers are exactly double those in 1:3. This shows God's care reaches even small details like the number of a man's cattle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Matthew Henry suggests the doubled prosperity may picture the glory of heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_042.cfm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: nothing could replace the children Job lost, but these ten were a true comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Catholic (Haydock): Job got twice everything except children, because his first children were living (Worthington) with God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job-42.html

**v. 14**
- Wesley on the names: Jemimah means "the day," for her beauty or because she was born after a dark night of affliction. Keziah is cassia, a fragrant spice. Keren-happuch means "plenty restored." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Guzik gives "Turtledove" or "Day-bright" for Jemimah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Haydock says the Septuagint renders the third name "Horn of Amalthea" (horn of plenty), which shows Job's abundance without approving the myth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job-42.html

**v. 15**
- Barnes says that among the Hebrews a daughter inherited only if there was no son (Numbers 27:8). That is why the detail is recorded, and it may imply equal shares. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/42-15.htm
- Clarke links it to Zelophehad's daughters. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/42-15.html
- Guzik sees a link to Job's godly conduct as a family man (Job 31). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-42/
- Wesley notes that women are praised for beauty in the Old Testament but never in the New, where the "beauty of holiness" comes into clearer light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Bible Hub's study note sees this as a picture of Christ giving all believers, of either sex, an inheritance. https://biblehub.com/job/42-15.htm

**v. 16**
- Wesley says some guess Job was seventy when his trouble came. If so, his age was doubled too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that the Septuagint gives 170 years after the calamity and 240 in total. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_042.cfm

**v. 17**
- Wesley says Job died as Eliphaz had described, like a ripe sheaf of corn in its season. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown add that "full of days" means fully satisfied. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/42.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_042.cfm
- The Greek Bible (Septuagint) adds lines saying Job will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up. It also identifies him with Jobab, a king of Edom. https://biblehub.com/sep/job/42.htm
- Haydock says this ending may preserve an ancient tradition, but the Church Fathers kept it separate from the inspired text. He also says Job can be seen as a lively figure of Christ; who was perfectly innocent, and yet a man of sorrows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job-42.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says nothing in Job shows he ruled Edom, and in Hebrew the names Job and Jobab have nothing in common. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08413a.htm
